questions.prompt: What is the first step of the debugging process in this lesson?
choices: Ask someone else to look at it
questions.explain: A bug you cannot make happen on demand cannot be confirmed fixed either. Reproducing it comes before any change to the code.

questions.prompt: Put the five steps of the debugging process in order.
items: Isolate the problem to a smaller piece of code
Verify the fix and check nothing else broke
Decide what should have happened instead
questions.explain: Reproduce, then know what correct looks like, then narrow down where it goes wrong, then fix, then verify. Fixing before you have isolated the problem is guessing.

questions.prompt: Which of these are debugging strategies this lesson recommends?
choices: Print variable values at different points
Change lines at random until the output looks right
Comment parts out to isolate the failing piece
questions.explain: The three chosen ones all narrow the search. Changing lines at random can make the symptom disappear while the bug stays, which is worse than not fixing it.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson say to compare expected against actual results?
choices: It makes the program run faster
Without knowing the right answer you cannot tell there is a bug at all
It replaces the need to test
questions.explain: A wrong answer only looks wrong next to the right one. That comparison is what turns 'it seems off' into a bug you can chase.

questions.prompt: A bug you cannot ___ consistently cannot be confirmed fixed either.
questions.explain: If the bug only appears sometimes, a fix that changes nothing looks exactly like a fix that worked.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Two things to weigh: what a bug costs if it survives, and what finding it early saves.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Walk the steps in order. The two that people skip are making the bug happen on demand first, and checking afterwards that nothing else broke.
